summary: Reports the work of an IAB advisory committee formed in 2003 to review how the IETF is administered, including its relationships with the RFC Editor, the IETF Secretariat and IANA, and to propose improvements. It did not look at the standards process itself. It is now marked historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Running the internet's rule-making was spread across several organizations with informal agreements between them. A committee set up in 2003 examined the arrangement and recommended a formal structure to replace it.

subtitle: How the IETF's leadership and supporting organizations worked together, and what an advisory committee found.

tldr.problem: The IETF's administration was spread across several organizations with informal relationships, while meeting attendance and therefore meeting income were falling and the budget was in deficit.
tldr.mechanism: An IAB Advisory Committee formed in September 2003 spent two months reviewing the IETF's relationships with the RFC Editor, the Secretariat and IANA, documented the stress points, set out requirements for resource management, stewardship and a working environment, and recommended a single formalized IETF organizational entity.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Informational memo from March 2004 and is now Historic. It records observations and advice only: the RFC states that its output represented no decision-making or implementation.

sections.title: The Advisory Committee and Its Mandate
sections.content:
In the fall of 2003, the IETF Chair and the IAB Chair formed an IAB Advisory Committee, the AdvComm, with a mandate to review the existing IETF administrative structure and relationships, which the memo lists as the RFC Editor, the IETF Secretariat and IANA, and to propose changes to the IETF management process or structure so that the IETF would function better. The mandate did not include the standards process itself.

The committee was formed in September 2003 and carried out its work over the following two months, before IETF58 in November 2003. Its membership included many of the people who had volunteered to manage the IETF's inter-organization administrative relationships in recent years, so the first phase of its work was sharing and discussing the tacit knowledge about those relationships. It then sought input from the other end of those relationships, which appears in the appendices of the RFC, and from that it drew a list of requirements for successful future IETF administration and finally put together advice on how the IETF might reorganize.

The memo is careful about what it is. It says the output does not represent any decision-making or implementation, that it documents the state of the committee's thinking at the end of a two month process, and that the next steps are review of the material by the community and specific proposals for action to be put forward by the IAB and IETF Chairs.
sections.plainLanguage: The two chairs of the IETF set up a committee in 2003 to look at how the organization was administered and to suggest changes. This document is what the committee found and what it advised.

sections.title: Who Does What Today
sections.content:
The memo separates the functions the IETF needs from the organizations that supply them, because in some cases one organization provides several services while the functions are logically distinct. The RFC Editor publishes the RFC document series and maintains the official standards status record. The Secretariat supports the IESG, the working groups, the community and the IETF meetings. IANA assigns protocol parameters and maintains the registries. Legal support, insurance and similar work is, in the committee's words, largely invisible and is provided by ISOC.

The committee also traced how those arrangements came about. ISOC has been the organizational home of the IETF since 1992. CNRI, founded in 1986, has provided IETF Secretariat services since 1987, and after ISOC was founded, ISOC assumed overall legal responsibility for the substantive workings of the IETF while CNRI assumed operational responsibility for the Secretariat; in 1998 the Secretariat was reorganized, placing its employees, including the IETF Executive Director, in a CNRI for-profit subsidiary, Foretec Seminars, Inc., founded in 1997. The RFC Editor activity is organized as a project within USC/ISI, using ISI infrastructure and supported by a contract with ISOC. ICANN, the non-profit corporation formed in 1998, took over the address space allocation, protocol parameter assignment, domain name system management and root server system management functions previously performed under a United States Government contract by IANA at ISI and other entities.

The money and people behind this work come from meeting fees collected through Foretec, contributions from ISOC members for standards, ICANN funding for IANA, and the time of volunteers and their employers: IETF participants, working group chairs, document editors, the IETF Nominating Committee, the IESG, the IAB and the IAB Executive Director.
sections.plainLanguage: Different organizations do different jobs: one runs the meetings, one publishes the documents, one keeps the list of protocol numbers, and one provides the legal cover. But the way they fitted together had grown over years rather than by design.

sections.title: The Stress Points
sections.content:
The committee found that the funding and operational structure depended on meeting attendance, and that the decline in that attendance, which had continued unabated, produced a decline in IETF revenue even as the requirements of IETF operation remained constant or increasing. The result was a budget deficit for operations that began in 2002 and was forecast to continue until at least 2004, even after a substantial increase in meeting fees, and the continuing deficits depleted working capital, making the IETF less robust against future budgetary disappointments.

The leadership also named other stressors that got in the way of solving the fiscal problems. The documentation of IETF processes and structure was in places vague about who was responsible for management and oversight, which made the arrangement opaque to the IETF community and sometimes left the leadership poorly placed to manage it, and the informality of the relationships with organizations carrying out key functions compounded that. Important institutional memory was recorded nowhere other than people's minds, which requires significant transmission of oral history for a leadership transition to be effective, and other important records were spread across various organizations, so finding the relevant documentation was challenging. Lack of automation in the basic request services had caused undue delay or failure in processing simple, routine tasks, even though automation itself needs resources and management.

The organizations that support the IETF reported the mirror-image problem: difficulty in determining authoritative channels for direction, whether through too many inputs or through no clear authority for resolving change requests. In the absence of written agreements they were not clear on whom to take direction from, and even where agreements existed the authority to give direction was not clear. The committee traced both problems to the same cause, that the IETF relies on external bodies for support but does not have sufficiently clear external relationships to state its requirements or its wishes about the services it wants.
sections.plainLanguage: Meeting income was falling while the work stayed the same, and the budget had been in deficit since 2002. On top of that, no one could say who was responsible for which part of the administration, and the supporting organizations did not know who to take direction from.

sections.title: Requirements for a Working Administration
sections.content:
The committee set out what the IETF needed. Under resource management, the IETF organization needed budgetary autonomy so it could make the hard choices about spending, with the leadership, advised and consented to by the community, taking them. It needed to treat all sources of income and all expenses as pieces of one budget, so it could adjust items when income from different sources varied, with the usual caveats that donations must not threaten the IETF's independence and that donations are easier when they are tax deductible. It needed clear contractual relationships with the organizations supporting basic services, including meeting organization, secretarial services and IT services, so that the distribution of rights, responsibilities and accountability is clear. It needed the ability to raise money for and fund the development of additional services, and it needed its needs met with a minimum of overhead, which implies combining work efforts and avoiding duplication.

Under stewardship, the administration needed to remain uniquely accountable to the IETF community, with responsibility for financial management sitting with people accountable inside the IETF organizational structure, and the distribution of responsibilities clear enough that the community can comment on current actions and future plans. History had to be documented properly, so the IETF needed to maintain and support the archiving of all of its working documents in a way that stays accessible to current and future workers, rather than relying on oral history.

Under the working environment, services should be automated wherever human judgment is not required, so that mechanical steps carry the least friction and the least delay. The committee noted that this is not a call to automate every process, but that reducing friction in the steps that are truly mechanical frees time and energy for the ones that need individual judgment. It also called for an adequately rich and consistent set of tools for the standards work.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements cover money, records and tools. The IETF needs to make its own spending decisions, treat all its income as one budget, hold written contracts with the organizations that do the work, keep durable archives, and automate the routine steps.

sections.title: A Single Formalized IETF Organization
sections.content:
The committee's advice was that the IETF be more formally organized. It recommended that the IETF become a single formalized organizational entity, so that it could take full responsibility for and management of the resources its work requires, provide and maintain the work environment it needs, and give proper stewardship of the institutional information the organization needs now and in future.

Whatever form that entity took, the committee set out some expectations. The administration would remain accountable to the IETF leadership and community, with the goal of clearer lines of responsibility and accountability. The formalized IETF would manage its financial resources directly and would be the direct signatory to agreements with other organizations, so it could negotiate and administer its own contracts. It would need a small staff complement, the committee's example being one full-time person, responsible to no other organization than the one chartered with the IETF's mission. The committee also named a non-goal: creating an entity that exists simply for the purpose of continuing to exist, so the change should be executed with the minimum formality needed to meet the requirements.

On the necessity of the change, the committee argued that an appropriately implemented formalization would permit the unification of resource management, decision making and stewardship, and that this is simply not possible to implement within the existing distributed and informal arrangement. It was equally clear that forming the organization does not immediately satisfy the requirements. The RFC puts it plainly: it is not a silver bullet, and changing the formal structure will not change the financial status of the IETF, but it would provide the basis on which the required decisions could be made and acted upon.
sections.plainLanguage: The group suggested making the IETF an official body that could sign its own contracts and control its own money, with a very small staff and no more ceremony than the job needs.

sections.title: Three Possible Structures
sections.content:
The committee was deliberately vague about the form the new entity should take and described three frameworks instead, noting that they are not complete proposals and that there is not enough detail to recommend a particular path.

The first is to keep the IETF as an activity of the Internet Society and define that relationship more tightly. Dedicated ISOC personnel would form the small staff complement and ISOC would become responsible for all the IETF's financial resources and expenses. This should be straightforward to implement, given ISOC's existing legal relationship with the IETF activity and its status as signatory for IETF-related contracts, and it fits the goal of minimizing formality. The question raised against it is that the general mission of ISOC is broader than the standardization activity of the IETF, and the ISOC Board of Trustees must stay focused on apportioning resources to meet that broader mission, so it is not clear that this approach gives the clear lines of responsibility the requirements call for.

The second is to create a legal not-for-profit subsidiary of ISOC with a mandate focused specifically on the IETF's mission. It would become the legal entity responsible for managing the IETF's resources and expenses and the signatory to other legal instruments on the IETF's behalf, and as a distinct legal entity it would be independently responsible for its own mission, which answers the concern that the IETF work might be disrupted by ISOC's wider obligations. It might have its own Board of Trustees composed of members appointed by the IETF and ISOC, though a board is not required, and it would continue to benefit from ISOC's infrastructure and support. It would take more work to create, because the subsidiary would have to be created and rights and responsibilities adjusted between it and ISOC.

The third is a completely autonomous entity, an IETF, Inc. or an IETF, LLC, created for the sole purpose of managing IETF administrative activities. This would offer complete autonomy with all the attendant rights and responsibilities, but an independent IETF would at a minimum have to operate much like a startup for the first few years, with the related financing and growth issues and survival risks. Given all the organizational change taking place in the same period, the committee believed the financial and political risks of such an approach should not be under-estimated: it would need initial working capital to cover the commitments for the first few meetings, a financing plan built on advance meeting fees would leave little margin for error, and working capital could not be assumed to come purely from corporate donations while staff to solicit them were not yet available. The impact on ISOC's ability to carry out its mission, and on the IETF's standing with governmental organizations, would also have to be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: The group set out three ways to do it: as a part of the Internet Society, as a separate company owned by the Internet Society, or as a completely independent company. It did not pick one, and it warned that the independent option carries the most money risk.

items.title: Resource management
items.text: Budgetary autonomy, one budget across all income and expenses, clear contracts with supporting organizations, and the least overhead possible.

items.title: Stewardship
items.text: An administration uniquely accountable to the IETF community, with clear responsibilities and archives that stay accessible.

items.title: Working environment
items.text: Automation of the steps that need no human judgment, and a richer, consistent set of tools for the standards work.
